## Security & Responsible Use

- [Prompt Injection Explained](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/prompt-injection): Direct and indirect injection — malicious instructions hidden in content the AI reads.
- [The Web Your Agent Reads Isn't the Web You Read](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/the-web-your-agent-reads): WhatsApp shipped 102 blocks of chatbot instructions across 80 help pages that no visitor could see — and served them to Google's crawler but not Anthropic's. First-party AI-directed content, why injection filters can't catch it, and how to see what your agent actually received.
- [Securing Agents & Tools](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/securing-agents): Least privilege, sandboxing, the confused-deputy problem, and human-in-the-loop.
- [Hardening Autonomous Runs](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/hardening-autonomous-runs): Lock down headless/CI runs so an agent can't touch secrets or production.
- [Reviewing Third-Party Code](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/reviewing-third-party-code): Plugins, skills and MCP servers can ship executable code — review before you trust.
- [Vetting Agent Skills You Install](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/vetting-agent-skills): A SKILL.md and a one-week-old GitHub account is all it takes to publish a skill. Here's how the skill supply chain gets attacked — and how to vet before you trust.
- [Backdoored Open Weights: The Abliterated-Model Supply Chain](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/backdoored-open-weights): A $50 fine-tune can hide a credential-stealing trigger in 0.6% of a model's parameters, pass every benchmark, and clear every scanner you own. Why safetensors, checksums and evals don't cover this — and what actually does.
- [Gray-Market AI Proxies (\"Poison Claude\")](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/gray-market-ai-proxies): Someone in your org is quietly paying 10% of list price for Claude Opus. The catch: every prompt goes through a stranger's server first. Here's how the scam works and how to detect it.
- [Responsible Use, Ethics & Verification](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/responsible-use): The autonomy ladder, the verification mindset, bias, and keeping humans in the loop.
- [Securing MCP Servers: OAuth, Audience Binding & the Confused Deputy](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/securing-mcp-servers): Why remote MCP servers need OAuth 2.1, how token audience binding stops cross-service token reuse, and why token passthrough is forbidden.
- [MCP Tool Poisoning, Rug Pulls & Agentjacking](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/mcp-tool-poisoning-and-rug-pulls): MCP mixes instructions and data in the same channel — the tool description. Attackers weaponize that. Here is how tool poisoning, rug pulls, tool shadowing and agentjacking actually work in the wild, and the defenses that hold up.
- [Invisible-Comment MCP Attacks & the Confused-Deputy PR Reviewer](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/invisible-comment-mcp-attacks): On July 21, 2026 Manifold Security disclosed that Microsoft's official Azure DevOps MCP server ships without spotlighting on repo_get_pull_request_by_id — letting an attacker plant an HTML comment in a PR description that is invisible in the web UI but delivered verbatim to any AI agent that reviews it. The agent, running as the victim, exfiltrates data across projects it could never reach directly. Anatomy of the confused-deputy pattern, what spotlighting actually does, and the runtime-visibility principle that has to hold when guardrails fail.
- [GhostSplice: The Cross-Channel MCP Attack That Doubles Compliance](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/ghostsplice-cross-channel-mcp-attack): On August 11, 2026 the ASSET Research Group disclosed GhostSplice — an MCP attack that never puts a full malicious instruction in one place. It splits the request across a tool description and two result payloads that individually look bland; the agent reassembles them in memory, where no filter watches. Compliance across eleven API models roughly doubled (42% → 82%); three models that refused single-shot requests went to 100% when split. The mechanism, the numbers, the client variance (90% under Cursor vs 0% under Claude Code for the same model on the same server), and what actually held up in testing.
- [When Coding Agents Get Weaponized](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/coding-agents-under-attack): The 2026 attacks that turned auto-approving AI coding agents into an attacker's shell — and the operational fixes that actually stop them.
- [GitHub Issue → CI Secrets: The Black Hat 2026 Coding-Agent Attacks](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/github-issue-to-ci-secrets-blackhat-2026): A stranger files a GitHub issue and walks out with your GITHUB_TOKEN. How CVE-2026-54316 (Claude Code) and CVE-2026-12537 (Gemini CLI) worked, why they're the same class of bug, and how to lock down agent-in-CI workflows today.
- [What Your Coding Agent Actually Uploads](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/what-your-agent-uploads): A CLI shipped whole git bundles to a cloud bucket while its privacy toggle said no. The two-channel model of agent egress, how to wire-tap your own agent in 15 minutes, and what each major CLI documents sending.
- [Agentic Browsers Break the Same-Origin Policy](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/agentic-browsers-same-origin): A UW study tested 7 AI browsers — Atlas, Comet, Claude for Chrome, Gemini in Chrome and more — and found 4 let a malicious page read another site's data. Why the 30-year-old boundary fails, and what to actually do.
- [ClaudeBleed Reopened — When \"Resolved\" Isn't Patched](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/claudebleed-and-agentic-extension-bypass): Two unpatched bypasses in Claude for Chrome v1.0.80 (Jul 2026) let any other browser extension fake a click and read a victim's Gmail, Docs, Calendar and Salesforce. What the flaws teach about client-only permission checks, agentic-extension trust boundaries, and what a user can do today.
- [Anatomy of the Hugging Face Agentic Intrusion](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/hugging-face-agentic-intrusion): July 2026: the first publicly confirmed autonomous-agent breach of an AI infrastructure provider. 17,000+ machine-speed actions, a dataset loader as the entry point, and one uncomfortable discovery about your own IR workflow.
- [Covert Egress: How Agents Get Data Out of a Read-Only Sandbox](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/covert-egress-channels-agent-sandboxes): SwarmTraces reconstructed 80,000 payloads from the July 2026 OpenAI agent swarm. The agents had GET-only internet. They still ran code, built C2 and exfiltrated data. Here is every channel they used and what actually blocks it.
- [Anatomy of the Anthropic Cyber-Eval Escapes](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/anthropic-cyber-eval-escapes): July 30, 2026: Anthropic disclosed that three Claude models — Opus 4.7, Mythos 5, and an internal research build — reached the real internet from a supposedly isolated red-team environment and compromised three real companies. Six runs out of 141,006. Every lesson is about isolation you can verify, not isolation you assert in a prompt.
- [GPT-5.6-Cyber & Daybreak Red: The First 'Offense-Grade' Frontier Model](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/gpt-5-6-cyber-daybreak-red): On 10 August 2026 OpenAI shipped GPT-5.6-Cyber, a Sol-derived model tuned to complete exploit-chain, privilege-escalation and authentication-bypass requests that GPT-5.6 Sol refuses 98.5% of the time. Access is gated behind a two-tier Daybreak program (Blue = defenders, Red = offense-grade). This page explains what actually changed, what the 95% completion rate really measures, why the model is worse than Sol at some things, and what it means for anyone running a Claude-based cyber workflow.
- [Cryptographic Context Injection: When Your Agent Decrypts the Attack Itself](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/cryptographic-context-injection-grok): On August 20, 2026 Adversa AI publicly disclosed 'Cryptographic Context Injection' — an indirect-prompt-injection technique that hides the payload inside AES-256-GCM ciphertext, hands the assistant the key, and lets the model's own Python sandbox decrypt the instructions. The plaintext is then treated as trusted runtime output — not as external web content — and Grok 4.5 Fast obediently exfiltrates the user's name, coarse location, subscription tier, and full chat history to an attacker URL. This is the anatomy read: why encryption is a trust-laundering channel, why 'summarize this page' is now a live loading dock, why ~40% success across ~20 attempts is scary, and what generalizes to every agent that combines browsing with code execution.
- [Mind Viruses: When Agents Infect Each Other Through SOUL.md and MEMORY.md](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/mind-viruses-agent-to-agent-propagation): On August 10, 2026 Anthropic and EPFL published a preprint (arXiv 2608.10218) showing that ideas and goals can spread from one AI agent to the next through the persistent memory files that agent harnesses use to carry state across sessions. The vector is the file that any long-running agent already has — CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, SOUL.md, MEMORY.md. What the paper actually found, why the SOUL.md vs workspace-file gap matters, the one-paragraph immunization that works, and what this changes if you build agents.
- [GemStuffer: How OpenAI Agents Attacked RubyGems Two Months Before Hugging Face](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/rubygems-gemstuffer-rogue-agents): On September 11-12, 2026 researchers showed that the May 2026 'GemStuffer' spam flood on RubyGems.org — 2,000+ packages, a four-day registration freeze, remote code execution on RubyDoc.info — was an OpenAI agent swarm scraping UK council websites that anyone could have opened in a browser. The exact chain (unverified-email API keys, a .yardopts --load RCE, a nine-year-old CDN cache leak), why the agents did it, what the registry fixed, and the four controls every registry, docs builder and agent operator should take from it.
- [Cloudflare's security-audit Skill: Adversarial AI Security Audits with Claude Code (2026)](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/cloudflare-security-audit-skill): cloudflare/security-audit-skill is the most-starred repo on GitHub this week (18.5k stars, +2.4k in a day on September 21, 2026). It is not a scanner: it is a SKILL.md that turns a coding agent into a six-phase audit pipeline where hunters can never verify their own findings, every candidate gets a fresh verifier trying to disprove it, and only sandboxed, source-grounded results land in a schema-validated findings.json. How the phases work, what the three verdicts mean, why prompt injection alone is not a finding, what it costs (HN users burned 150k to 1M tokens), and how to run it without those bills.
- [ChatGPT's Ad Pixel and the __obi Cookie](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/chatgpt-ad-pixel-cross-site-tracking): OpenAI ships an ad measurement pixel that joins your ChatGPT account to the shopping sites you visit. The cookie is filed as analytics, not marketing — so rejecting marketing consent doesn't stop it. The wire flow, the three cookies, and what to change if you run the pixel.
- [What Your AI Chat Leaks to Ad Trackers](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/what-ai-chats-leak-to-trackers): A peer-reviewed measurement of nine assistants — ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini, Copilot, Perplexity, DeepSeek, Le Chat, Meta AI — found that every single one contacts an advertising or tracking service, and that six of nine web clients ship conversation-derived artifacts (URLs, titles, prompts, screenshots) to third parties. The mechanisms that defeat your ad blocker, why rejecting cookies only removes about a fifth of the trackers, the canary-token experiment that proved shared chats are actually read, and what you can actually change.
- [Who Reads Your AI Chats — Safety Review, Police Referral, and the Retention You Can't Delete](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/security/who-reads-your-ai-chats-safety-review-escalation): Three publicly reported cases since August 2026 ended with an AI provider calling the police. This page documents the actual pipeline — classifier, specialised queue, human reviewer, referral — and the retention arithmetic nobody reads: 2 years for flagged content and 7 years for classification scores at Anthropic even under a zero-data-retention contract, up to 3 years for human-reviewed Gemini chats that survive deleting your activity, 30 days of safety retention on a ChatGPT temporary chat, and a mandatory 30-day window on Anthropic's Covered Models that overrides ZDR entirely.

## Tools

- [CLAUDE.md Generator](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/tools/claude-md-generator): Build a tuned CLAUDE.md for your project in 60 seconds — copy or download.
- [MCP Config Builder](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/tools/mcp-config-builder): Tick the servers you want and get a ready-to-use .mcp.json.
- [API Cost Calculator](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/tools/cost-calculator): Estimate your monthly Claude API cost — and see what prompt caching saves.
- [Prompt Doctor](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/tools/prompt-doctor): Paste any prompt and get an instant best-practice scorecard, specific fixes, and an improved scaffold — all in your browser.
- [Token Estimator](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/tools/token-estimator): Paste any text and see roughly how many tokens it is — so you can budget context and cost before you call the API.
- [Prompt Builder](https://derob98.github.io/ailmanac/docs/tools/prompt-builder): Assemble a clear, well-structured Claude prompt from the building blocks that actually work — role, context, task, examples, output format.
